data.title: Taiwan's Stock Pickers Are Walking Out to Bet Their Own Money
data.description:
NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly On Wall Street News Commentary - Taiwan's benchmark stock index was up 62% this year, the best showing of any major equity gauge in the world, when Bloomberg reported on Oct. 16 that some of the island's professional fund managers and analysts are quitting their jobs to invest their own money. Strict rules keep them from trading the very stocks they pick for clients, and in a year when about one in ten stocks in the index has more than doubled, some have decided the trade-off is no longer worth it. Companies and funds mentioned in this article include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited ( TSM ) [TSMC] , ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. ( ASX ) [ASE] , United Microelectronics Corporation ( UMC ) [UMC] , iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF , The Taiwan Fund, Inc. ( TWN ) .

Watching From Behind the Locker

Taiwan does not ban personal investing outright, but its asset-management code of conduct bars staff from trading a locally listed stock or a linked derivative within seven business days before or after their firm's funds trade it, which in practice rules out personal stock-picking. Fund managers must also lock away their phones, laptops and smartwatches each morning until the market closes at 1:30 p.m. The phone rule was formalized in 2024 to deter insider trading, the Taipei Times reported in July, after six former fund managers from four firms were indicted for front-running trades through the accounts of relatives and friends.

Ken Tsai, 40, a fund manager who until July worked at a large Taiwanese asset manager that Bloomberg did not name, told Bloomberg he made a Taiwanese maker of AI-server data-transfer components his fund's largest holding in 2024. The stock rose more than fivefold in 2025 and about sixfold again this year, but he owned none of it personally. "It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation," he said. He now works at a private investment firm in Taipei, which was also not named. Pay adds to the pull: Taiwan portfolio managers earn roughly US$124,000 to US$311,000 a year, well below Hong Kong base salaries, according to Bloomberg, citing headhunters and recruitment-firm data.

The private shops they are joining sit outside those rules. They register as private companies with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and do not need asset-management licenses from the Financial Supervisory Commission because they do not raise public money. Brokers told Bloomberg some of them now generate more than NT$10 billion in monthly trading volume, rivaling mid-sized asset managers.

The Rally Behind the Exits

Much of the rally traces back to the AI hardware supply chain. TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (US$46.7 billion) on Oct. 15, up 50.9% from a year earlier, while net income jumped 68.7% and gross margin reached 66.4%. It guided fourth-quarter revenue from US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion.

Chip packaging and testing has ridden the same wave. ASE Technology ( ASX ) reported September net revenue of NT$88.1 billion, up 45.5% from a year earlier, and third-quarter revenue of NT$244.2 billion, up 44.8%.

Mature-node foundry UMC reported August sales up 30.71% from a year earlier, lifting year-to-date sales 14.66%. In its second-quarter report, the company guided for capacity utilization above 90% in the third quarter and said revenue from its 22/28nm business continues to set record highs.

CONTINUED... Read more market coverage at: flyonwallstreet.com

A Talent Squeeze, Not a Stampede

The numbers point to churn more than an exodus. Fewer than half of Taiwan's 20 largest local equity mutual funds have kept the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data site MoneyDJ, and Bloomberg reported that applications for junior roles at some international firms have roughly halved this year. Yet the FSC said the industry's registered headcount actually rose to 4,729 in September from 4,581 at the end of 2025. Firms are responding: the largest foreign asset manager in Taiwan is offering cross-market analyst roles and office rotations to keep staff.

Regulators are paying attention. The FSC said on Oct. 15 it is gathering information and plans to review the rules, balancing market development against conflicts of interest and investor protection. One asset-management executive told Bloomberg there is no easy solution for now.

The Case for the Pros

At least one professionally managed fund has kept pace. The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ), a closed-end fund listed in New York, reported a 47.36% total return for its fiscal quarter ended May 31, against 26.12% for the TAIEX Total Return Index over the same period, with net asset value of US$116.90 a share at the end of that quarter.

Investors who prefer to own the whole market can use the iShares MSCI Taiwan ETF, which holds about US$11.9 billion in assets.

Last week was a reminder of how quickly the math can change. The TAIEX fell 4.6%, its first weekly decline in five weeks, as a technology selloff spread and TSMC CEO C.C. Wei warned of macroeconomic uncertainty and weak consumer demand, according to Trading Economics. In New York, TSMC's shares fell 8.98% from the Oct. 9 close to $412.61 on Oct. 16, ASE dropped 14.86% to $39.53, UMC slid 13.68% to $19.82, the iShares fund lost 7.04% to $106.26 and The Taiwan Fund ( TWN ) declined 8.78% to $94.18, according to Stock Analysis data. For the managers who just traded a salary for their own account, those swings now land on them.

data.title: FTSE 100 posts weekly loss as AI jitters spark risk-off move
data.description:
(Updates after markets close)

Nov 6 (Reuters) - Britain's FTSE 100 fell 1% on Friday after touching a more than three-week low earlier in the session and registered a weekly decline, as AI jitters following Democrats' capture of the US Congress sparked a broad risk-off move.

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell 1.01% to 10,673.94 points and was down 0.5% for the week, while the midcap FTSE 250 slipped 0.80%, but still eked out a tiny weekly gain.

* The Democrats' capture of the US House and Senate earlier this week sparked concerns of AI regulation, a slowdown in data-centre buildouts and hyperscalers tightening their purse strings

* The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq indexes traded higher on Friday, after posting on Thursday their sharpest one-day falls since April 2025

* "When $2.5 trillion of value is lost from one of the major US stock market indices in a day, it's understandable that investors are feeling on edge," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell

* The jitters spilled over to global markets, with the European benchmark STOXX 600 ending 1% lower

* Most sectors in London slid, with precious metal miners being an exception and rising 1.7%

* Telecom stocks dropped 3.6%, leading the declines in the index, with BT Group and Airtel Africa ( AAFRF ) sliding 6.4% and 4%, respectively

* Traditionally defensive sectors such as pharma and personal care, drug and groceries also slid around 0.6% and 1.7%, respectively, highlighting the breadth of the market retreat

* Oil prices slipped on Friday, weighing on energy stocks, which ended down 1.6%

* Separately, Lloyds said British house prices fell at the fastest annual pace in a year in October as higher mortgage costs weighed on demand

* Man Group ( MNGPF ) was the biggest faller on the FTSE 250 with a 7.6% drop after Kuwait's public pension fund on Thursday won a lawsuit against the asset manager

(Reporting by Darshan Kumar, Purvi Agarwal and Anand Gopal in Bengaluru; Editing by Harikrishnan Nair and Xevi Fontdegloria)

  • Public Utilities Commission of Ohio on May 13, 2026; and

data.title: US labor market regains ground as job growth surges, unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US job growth accelerated in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, suggesting that the labor market could be strengthening after stumbling in mid-summer and keeping the Federal Reserve on track to raise interest rates in December.

The Labor Department's closely watched employment report on Friday also showed the economy added 84,000 more jobs in August and September than previously reported. The decline in the unemployment rate from 4.2% in September was despite more people piling into the labor force, likely seeking to cushion themselves against higher living costs resulting from the conflict in the Middle East.

The better-than-expected report followed on the heels of data this week showing a rise in job openings in September, which combined with historically low layoffs has raised the specter of the labor market tightening.

"The labor market is heating up across-the-board and supports our view that the Fed will raise the policy rate again in December," said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide.

Nonfarm payrolls jumped by 165,000 jobs last month after an upwardly revised 60,000 gain in September, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls advancing 65,000 after a previously reported 29,000 increase in September.

Estimates ranged from 35,000 to 125,000 jobs. August's employment gains were revised up to 186,000 from the previously estimated 133,000. Employment growth averaged 137,000 over the last three months compared to an average loss of 45,000 during the same period in 2025. Some economists were skeptical of the labor market's newfound strength.

"Recent improvements in the employment situation largely relate to a major jump in federal government spending in the third quarter, as well as an unprecedented surge in election spending reported to be near $12 billion within a relatively short time frame of August to October," said Brian Bethune, an economics professor at Boston College.

Last month's broad-based increase in payrolls was led by the professional and business services industry, which added 70,000 jobs, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past 12 months. Those jobs were in professional, scientific and technical services as well as administrative and support, waste management and remediation services.

Healthcare employment increased by 42,000 jobs, mostly at hospitals and home healthcare services. The transportation and warehousing sector added 25,000 positions, the majority of them couriers and messengers, consistent with strong domestic demand.

Manufacturing payrolls rose by 19,000 jobs, spread across computer and electronic products, machinery and primary metals. The increases are likely linked to the artificial intelligence buildout. There were modest job gains in the retail, financial activities and government sectors.

CONSTRUCTION LOSES JOBS

Construction shed 3,000 jobs, the bulk of them residential specialty trade contractors. Residential building construction employment also declined against the backdrop of high mortgage rates, which have depressed homebuilding. Home renovations have also been trending down.

Leisure and hospitality employment dropped by 13,000 positions, concentrated in the accommodation and food services sector. The share of industries reporting growth last month increased to 57.6% from 54.2% in September. The average workweek was unchanged at 34.4 hours.

Financial markets priced in a roughly 80% chance of a rate hike at the US central bank's meeting next month, up from 66.9% on Thursday, CME's FedWatch tool showed.

The Fed last week left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range. Next Tuesday's consumer inflation report for October could offer more clues on the course of monetary policy in early 2027. Economists are also watching the stock market after a tech-sector rout on Thursday amid fears a Democratic-led Congress could lead to tougher AI regulation.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading higher. The dollar gained versus a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields rose.

Economists estimated the economy needs to create at least 40,000 jobs per month to keep up with growth in the working-age population. The so-called breakeven rate has declined from roughly 150,000 in 2024 because of the smaller labor force as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration.

Household employment, a volatile measure, increased 463,000 in October, outpacing the 421,000 people who entered the labor force. About 1.589 million people have joined the labor force over the past three months, lifting the participation rate to 61.9% from 61.6% in August. But many of them, mostly re-entrees, have not found work.

Young adults have virtually been locked out of the labor market, with AI eliminating some entry-level positions.

The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.9 weeks, the longest since November 2021, from 11.5 weeks in September. There were more people working part-time for economic reasons last month, with the number increasing 339,000 to 4.840 million.

A broader measure of unemployment, which includes people who want to work but have given up searching and those working part-time because they cannot find full-time ⁠employment, rose to 7.9% from 7.6% in September. Historically low layoffs have anchored the labor market.

Though hiring is picking up, it has lagged economic growth, with gross domestic product increasing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter. Economists said uncertainty from the US-Israeli war with Iran as well as the impact of AI on staffing needs had left businesses hesitant to increase head count.

"More than a quarter of unemployed workers were searching for six months or longer in October, a share rarely seen outside the aftermath of a recession," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab. "And even when employers do hire, job posting data suggests that they have increasingly tilted their hiring toward experience, leaving people early in their careers with even fewer ways in."

Wage growth maintained its moderate pace, increasing 3.1% in the 12 months through October after advancing 3.2% in September. While that underscored the disinflationary impulse from the labor market, it illustrated the continued erosion of household incomes. Consumer prices rose 3.7% year-on-year in September.

Anger over inflation resulted in President Donald Trump's Republican Party losing control of Congress to Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections.

"The American public will continue to skeptically look at the current economic expansion which is highly skewed towards upper- end households and corporates that are profiting from strong underlying demand and robust non-residential investment," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM.

(Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Andrea Ricci)

data.title: Tesla to pull the plug on Cybertruck after years of poor sales
data.description:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Musk's pet projects. In an X post, Musk said the wind-down would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotaxi he has made central to the automaker's autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday's US midterm elections, with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.

Combined, his companies were on track to lose more than $180 billion in market capitalization for the week.

While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the specialized components for the heavy, angular model.

In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era."

Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

The US EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.

"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same."

"It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves."

Musk's SpaceX was one of the model's biggest customers last year and bought Cybertrucks worth $131 million from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.

'CYBERTRUCK WON'T GO, CAN'T GO'

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.

The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them.

During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future."

But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.

Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market.

"All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said.

But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.

"Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said.

MUSK'S NEW BET

The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.

Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit in September to review the basis for that certification.

"Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

However, the Cybercab is unlikely to make up for lost Cybertruck volumes soon. The two-seater robotaxi is still a small program, with production beginning only earlier this year. Tesla has listed an installed capacity of more than 125,000 units.

About 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis operating in Texas are Cybercabs, with the rest mainly Model Y vehicles, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles.

(Reporting by Ananya Palyekar, Akanksha Khushi and Akash Sriram in Bengaluru; Editing by Jochelle Mendonca, Janane Venkatraman, Raju Gopalakrishnan and Jonathan Ananda)

data.title: EMERGING MARKETS-Latam stocks, currencies gain; Mexico peso rebounds after Banxico cut
data.description:
* Analysts cut Argentina's 2026 growth forecast, bump up inflation outlook

* Argentina markets shut for public holiday

* Mexican peso recovers after surprise rate cut triggered losses

* Strong US jobs data revives bets on a Fed rate hike next month

(Updates with late afternoon trading)

By Sudeshna Ghoshal, Ragini Mathur and Avinash P

Nov 6 (Reuters) - Most Latin American stocks and currencies edged higher on Friday, and were poised to wrap up the week on a strong note as investors weighed the US midterm election results, a strong US jobs report and regional central bank policy signals.

MSCI's Latin American currency index was muted, but was set for a second consecutive weekly loss. The regional equities index gained 0.6%, though it was marginally lower for the week and on track to extend its losing run to four straight weeks.

Investors also assessed US Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm elections on Tuesday, which fueled hopes of a de-escalation in the war with Iran, helping push crude prices sharply lower. But concerns that the new Democratic-controlled Congress could subject AI infrastructure build out to greater scrutiny hit technology shares, while a broader risk-off mood weighed on other markets.

In the region, Mexico's peso rose 0.6%, recovering some losses triggered on Thursday after Banxico, as the country's central bank is also called, unexpectedly cut its benchmark rate by 25 basis points. The bank called the move a "one-time adjustment."

Analysts said the peso's turnaround post the rate cut reflected growing optimism that changes to the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) could face greater scrutiny after the U.S. midterm elections, easing concerns about Mexico's trade relationship with its largest export market.

"When it comes to the USMCA trade agreement, it has always been stipulated that any changes or amendments have to pass by Congress. The idea is now that the White House is going to be having tremendous opposition," said Juan Perez, director of trading at Monex.

"If that's not going to be the case, that's very good news for both of those countries and will translate into protection for the Mexican peso. That development absolutely overshadows the very idea of loose monetary policy."

The peso was on track for modest weekly gains, which would snap an eight-week losing streak driven by uncertainty over US trade talks and dovish minutes from the central bank's policy meeting in September.

Mexican shares were up 0.3%, rising for a third day and heading for a weekly advance.

Separately, stronger-than-expected US jobs report reinforced expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike next month, with the dollar rising 0.8% against a basket of currencies.

MODEST REBOUND IN BRAZIL

Brazil's real was trading flat against the dollar. The central bank on Wednesday paused its easing cycle, holding rates steady amid a worsening inflation outlook following President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's reelection last month.

Brazil's top lenders have slashed their economic growth forecasts for next year, threatening reelected President Lula's pledge to honor his campaign spending promises while also returning the budget to surplus.

The Bovespa gained 1.2% and was set for a modest weekly rise after a steep selloff last week.

In Argentina, a central bank survey on Thursday showed analysts lowering their 2026 growth forecasts while raising inflation expectations. Local markets were closed for a public holiday.

Chile's peso inched 0.2%, while the country's stock index climbed 0.7%. Consumer prices rose 0.5% in October from the prior month, accelerating from the 0.4% increase in September as fuel costs climbed, though the reading came in below forecasts.

(Updates throughout)

* Indexes: Dow down slightly, S&P 500 up 0.7%, Nasdaq up 1.5%

* Semiconductors bounce back from worst day in six years

* October jobs report surprises to the upside

By Colin Barr and Shashwat Chauhan

Nov 6 (Reuters) - Technology stocks bounced back on Friday from their worst drubbing in more than a year, but the Nasdaq Composite index was on track for a fourth consecutive weekly decline as investors sifted for clues about what comes next in the AI trade.

Gains within technology were broadly shared, with the semiconductor index up 4.4% and Nvidia ( NVDA ), Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) and Sandisk ( SNDK ) rebounding.

The broad revival underscores investor faith in the AI buildout that has driven US stock indexes to dozens of record closes this year, despite a shakeout that began with a US long-term Treasury yield spike in August and the stock volatility of the past month.

"We still think AI is the dominant theme in this bull market," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta. "We are still giving technology the benefit of the doubt."

At 2:10 p.m. ET (1910 GMT), the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off 20 points at 51,502, the S&P 500 was up 58 points, or 0.7%, at 7,411 and the Nasdaq Composite was up 365 points, or 1.5%, at 24,682.

Lerner said he views the selloff this week, which has taken the Nasdaq down 3% and put it in correction territory denoting a 10% decline from its peak a month ago, as likely offering a longer-term buying opportunity for many investors.

"AI has gone on trial several times in this cycle and come away with an innocent verdict," said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial in Charlotte, North Carolina. Referring to the election results that spurred heavy selling in AI stocks, he said, "This week we saw a little bit of a knee-jerk reaction."

Six of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were trading higher, with information technology leading gains. Consumer staples and healthcare were the laggards. The benchmark index was on pace for its worst week since June.

US nonfarm payrolls increased more than expected in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, suggesting the labor market remained resilient. Traders added to bets that the Federal Reserve could hike rates as soon as next month, with a 78% chance of a December move compared with a 70% chance seen earlier.

"Those are strong numbers," said Joe Saluzzi, co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading. But "will the Fed want to raise interest rates in the face of a market which is teetering?"

Tesla and SpaceX were among technology shares bouncing back from Thursday's plunge. Among other stock movers, software firm Atlassian ( TEAM ) dropped after reporting first-quarter results. Airbnb ( ABNB ) climbed after the vacation rental platform raised full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast.

Oil prices were slightly lower, adding to the bullish sentiment for riskier assets, and were on track for sharp weekly declines. The S&P 500 energy index was on track for a double-digit weekly percentage drop.

Despite the turbulence, Turnquist said a bullish sign for the AI buildout is the performance of copper, a major ingredient in data center buildouts and other technology. Copper futures remain above their 200-day moving average and their September lows, he said, despite the stock selling.

"If this is real demand destruction on AI, you'd think copper would start to roll over," Turnquist said. "It's not a perfect barometer, but I look at it as a reality check."

(Reporting by Colin Barr in New York, Shashwat Chauhan and Utkarsh Hathi in Bengaluru; Editing by Saumyadeb Chakrabarty, Arun Koyyur, Joyjeet Das, Rod Nickel)

data.title: Four things to note from Friday's US jobs report
data.description:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October - 100,000 more than expected by economists - and the unemployment rate ticked down unexpectedly to 4.1% amid a fairly broad-based improvement in the job market.

Here is a look at four notable data points from the Bureau of Labor Statistics report.

FOREIGN-BORN WORKERS LEAD GAINS

The US labor force had contracted notably during President Donald Trump's first year back in office, and economists connected the large outflows of foreign-born workers that led the decline to Trump's immigration crackdown. Recently that has been reversing.

The workforce has expanded sharply in the last three months in particular, and all of the net gains in labor force participation and employment -- as measured by the payrolls report's household survey -- have come from foreign-born workers. Employment and participation among native-born workers have fallen since July.

MANUFACTURING COMEBACK

Factory work is another corner of the job market experiencing a U-turn to the upside. In Trump's first year, the manufacturing sector shed 93,000 jobs even as he imposed tariffs on imported goods to try to boost domestic factory employment.

That decline began reversing this year, and since December 2025 the sector has added 101,000 jobs, leading to a net gain of 8,000 factory jobs since Trump returned to the White House.

JOBLESS FOR LONGER

The recent uptick in the pace of hiring has not yet begun to shorten the length of time that people who lose a job are out of work. While layoffs remain subdued and job gains have been sufficient in number to lower the unemployment rate, those with the misfortune of losing a job on average are remaining out of work for longer than any time in the past five years.

Excluding the short-lived surge in unemployment during the COVID-19 pandemic, both the median and average duration of unemployment -- 11.9 weeks and 27.1 weeks, respectively -- are the longest in about a decade.

AI IMPACTS

Most economists agree that the ever-widening adoption of artificial intelligence tools by employers has yet to produce major job displacements across the economy. That doesn't mean they are entirely absent.

"The most AI-exposed sectors, information and finance, continued to struggle and have shed jobs on a trend basis," Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, noted following the jobs report. "By contrast, professional and business services, which also has high AI adoption, bucked that trend and added 70,000 jobs in October while seeing upward revisions to past months. Those gains were broad, spanning temporary help and management and technical consulting services."

​

(Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci )

data.title: Private equity-owned landlord to pay $49.8 million over hidden fees
data.description:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - Progress Residential, the biggest US manager of single family rental homes, will pay $49.8 million to settle allegations by the Federal Trade Commission and four states that it deceived renters with hidden fees, an FTC official told Reuters on Friday.

The action builds on the FTC's work tackling corporate cost of living issues, as it explores requiring landlords to list mandatory fees and charges upfront as part of advertised rental rates.

Progress violated the law with charges, such as smart home fees or fees for lack of renters' insurance, that were not included in advertised rental rates, the FTC official said.

Roughly 35% of Americans rent their homes. According to a survey by Zillow, 60% of renters paid a recurring fee on top of rent last year.

Progress also routinely failed to return renters' security deposits and advertised homes as "move-in ready" that were in need of serious cleaning or repairs, the official said.

The FTC is receiving $48.5 million, which it will use to reimburse harmed consumers, and Arizona is receiving $1.25 million, the official said. Colorado, Indiana, and Utah were also expected to join the settlement.

Progress is a subsidiary of Pretium, a real-estate focused investment firm that owns and manages more than 82,000 rental homes across the US.

The company founded by former Goldman Sachs executive Don Mullen has said it aims to become one of the biggest homebuilding lenders by 2027.

Invitation Homes ( INVH ), another owner of single family rental homes launched in the wake of the subprime mortgage crisis, agreed to pay $48 million to settle an FTC action over hidden fees in 2024.

data.title: Daly says Fed rate hike likely, despite 'painful' tech-stock dive
data.description:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco President Mary Daly said on Friday she feels the US central bank will likely need to raise rates further to bring too-high inflation down, even as she acknowledged what she called the "painful" but orderly repricing of technology stocks as investors reassess the risks to AI-driven demand growth.

"My expectation is, we're going to have to tighten policy further," Daly said on CNBC, though exactly when and how much is not yet clear. Noting "how volatile the world seems to be in many ways," she added, "those volatilities are something that you have to take into account, collect more information, and be deliberate but more gradual in how you get there when you don't know exactly where you're going to need to head. But more is likely to be needed and certainly we're prepared --  I'm prepared -- to do that, if that's what the economy calls for."

(Reporting by Ann Saphir; Editing by Chris Reese)

data.title: Lawyer for Fed's Cook seeks clarity ahead of any White House hearing
data.description:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's lawyer has asked the White House to address fairness and process concerns before she attends a hearing that President Donald Trump wants held to assess whether he should fire her, even as one of the conveners said on Friday that it would go forward on December 14 as planned.

Trump has for more than a year been trying to remove Cook over mortgage fraud allegations that she denies and maintains are a pretense to oust her over her monetary policy decisions.

The Supreme Court in June ruled Trump cannot fire a Fed governor "at will" but may be able to do so for cause, if there is an opportunity for a defense. Trump's top economic aide, Kevin Hassett, has said the proposed hearing, which the president initially set for November 5, is designed to provide just that.

A White House official had told Reuters on Wednesday that the hearing had been rescheduled for December 14.

"There are no further changes to the schedule right now," Hassett told Reuters when asked if the White House will proceed with the hearing over objections from Cook's legal team.

Cook's lawyers have said she could be available if certain issues are addressed by the time the hearing is held, including the neutrality of the committee holding it, the "disclosure of any evidence they want to address, and roles of others in the process," a representative for her legal team told Reuters on Thursday, adding that her counsel has asked the White House to resolve those concerns.

Cook's lawyer, Abbe Lowell, had previously raised questions over whether the hearing, part of a White House investigation into Cook to be led by Hassett and two other Trump appointees, would be fair.

(Reporting by Ann Saphir, Bo Erickson and Trevor Hunnicutt; Editing by Jonathan Spicer and Paul Simao)

data.title: Sector Update: Tech Stocks Rise Friday Afternoon
data.description:
01:31 PM EST, 11/06/2026 (MT Newswires) -- Tech stocks were higher Friday afternoon, with the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) rising 1% and the State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) adding 3.2%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor index climbed up 2.6%.

In sector news, some prospective investors in Anthropic's initial public offering are discussing a valuation of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, down from previous estimate of $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion, Bloomberg reported. The Nasdaq index has plunged since the original estimate, including a 6.4% drop on Thursday.

Separately, OpenAI will continue to invest in AI infrastructure despite voter pushback against data centers during the midterm elections, CNBC reported, citing CFO Sara Friar. "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told the media outlet, according to the report. Friar indicated that OpenAI had built relationships with hyperscalers, and "it will continue to mean that we raise capital," the report said.

In corporate news, Alphabet (GOOGL) has built a stake worth about $547.9 million in Qualcomm ( QCOM ) , according to a regulatory filing. Alphabet shares were up 1%, and Qualcomm ( QCOM ) rose past 4%.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM ) is weighing whether to expand into the advanced memory chip manufacturing sector, as a shortage of memory chips has sent prices soaring and driven chip designers to look for additional supplies, The Information reported. Shares rose past 5%.

SpaceX (SPCX) could face a delay in discussions involving a potential purchase of state-owned land after Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa asked state officials to refrain from taking action during her transition to office, Bloomberg reported. SpaceX shares were up 6.6%.

data.title: REV Exploration Gets Final Approval for CSE Listing; Begins to Complete Operations at Aden Dome Helium Discovery
data.description:
01:25 PM EST, 11/06/2026 (MT Newswires) -- REV Exploration ( REVFF ) received final approval from the Canadian Securities Exchange to list its common shares on the CSE, it said Friday.

The shares will start trading on the CSE at market open on Nov. 9, with no change in the trading symbol or the CUSIP/ISIN, said the company.

REV Exploration ( REVFF ) also received approval to voluntarily delist its shares from the TSX Venture Exchange. The shares will be delisted from the TSXV at the close of market on Nov. 6, it added.

"The move to the CSE is a sensible step for a company at REV's stage, with no change to our trading symbol and nothing required of our shareholders," said Chief Executive Officer Jordan Potts. "It trims our overhead and keeps our focus on our Helium projects across the Northern Great Plains."

The company also said a service rig started completion operations at the Aden Dome helium discovery along the Alberta-Montana border.

The company's shares were last seen up CA$0.18, or 16.2%, at CA$1.29 on the TSX Venture Exchange.
